sections.h2: Where is the Franklin County Register of Deeds?
sections.html:
The Franklin County Register of Deeds is at 283-B S. Bickett Boulevard in Louisburg, NC 27549, after a move made while the county courthouse is under construction. The mailing address is P.O. Box 545, Louisburg, NC 27549, the phone is 919-496-3500 and the fax is 919-496-1457.

The county describes the office as the custodian of real estate documents for Franklin County that reach back to 1776. If you are selling a house anywhere in Franklin County, this is the office that holds the deed you received, the deed of trust on it and any plat or power of attorney tied to the parcel. Credit card payments are available. Because the office relocated recently, check the county page before you drive over with a document, and mail or e-record when you can.

sections.h2: What records does the Franklin County office keep?
sections.html:
It keeps the public land records for the county plus vital records, and the two groups are handled at the same counter. For a home sale the land records matter most.

  • Deeds and deeds of trust, the documents that move title and secure a loan.
  • Powers of attorney, assumed names, maps and other papers connected to real property.
  • Military discharge records.
  • Birth and death certificates back to 1913 for events in Franklin County, and marriage certificates back to 1869, with a bond book that carries marriage information from 1779.

The office can also print birth and death certificates from the state system for North Carolina events, and it takes online orders for certified or regular copies of vital records through a county vendor. A seller dealing with an inherited house often needs a death certificate and the old deed from the same visit.

sections.h2: Does Franklin County require tax certification before a deed is recorded?
sections.html:
Yes. Since April 1, 2015 the Register of Deeds will not accept a deed that transfers real property unless the Franklin County Tax Collector has certified that no delinquent property taxes or other taxes the administrator collects are a lien on it.

The Collections Department provides the certification at no charge on weekdays from 8 am to 5 pm, excluding county holidays. You can stop by with the deed before recording. By mail, address the request to the Franklin County Tax Collector, P.O. Box 503, Louisburg, NC 27549, Attention: Tax Certification. Deeds sent through eRecording are routed to the tax office by the electronic system. The county notes a 4:30 pm cutoff for electronic recordings that need the tax certification stamp, so a closing that ends late in the afternoon should send the package early.

For a seller with back taxes, this step is where the problem shows up. The deed does not get recorded until the delinquent balance is cleared or the closing agent pays it from the proceeds.

sections.h2: Can I record a Franklin County deed electronically?
sections.html:
Yes. The office accepts every document type by eRecording except UCC filings, and title companies, banks, attorneys and private individuals can submit that way.

The county lists three authorized providers to contact: CSC eRecording Solutions at 866-652-0111, Simplifile at 800-460-5657 and ePN, the eRecording Partners Network, at 888-325-3365. The county says electronic filing can mean faster recording, lower postage and courier cost, fewer rejected documents and more document security. A closing attorney usually picks the provider, so a seller rarely has to set this up personally, but it is worth asking your attorney whether the closing will be recorded electronically and on what day.

sections.h2: What does it cost to record a deed and what is the transfer tax?
sections.html:
The recording fee comes from a uniform statewide schedule, and the transfer tax is separate and is based on the price.

Under G.S. 161-10, an ordinary instrument costs $26.00 for the first 15 pages plus $4.00 for each extra page, and a deed of trust or mortgage costs $64.00 for the first 35 pages plus $4.00 for each extra page. Satisfactions and cancellations of a deed of trust carry no fee. A certified copy is $5.00 for page one and $2.00 for each added page, and a nonstandard document adds $25.00.

The excise tax on a deed under G.S. 105-228.30 is $1.00 on each $500.00 or fractional part of the consideration or value of the interest conveyed. The transferor pays it to the register of deeds before the instrument is recorded. Half goes to the county general fund and the rest is remitted to the Department of Revenue. In a normal sale the seller pays this at closing, so ask your closing attorney for the exact figure on your settlement statement.

sections.h2: Who handles each step when I sell in Franklin County?
sections.html:
Several county offices touch a sale, and each one has a different job. The table shows the split using the county's own descriptions.

Franklin County offices and the part each plays in a sale
OfficeWhat it doesContact
Register of DeedsRecords the deed and deed of trust, keeps land records and collects the recording fees919-496-3500
Collections Department (Tax Collector)Collects property tax and certifies there is no delinquent tax before a deed is recorded919-496-2172
Tax AdministrationSets values and handles real estate value appealsCounty Tax Office, through the Value Appeals page
eRecording providerSends the signed documents to the Register of Deeds electronicallyCSC, Simplifile or ePN

Sources for the table are the county Register of Deeds, Collections, Value Appeals and Electronic Recording pages listed below.

sections.h2: When are Franklin County property taxes due and what happens on a sale?
sections.html:
Franklin County real estate tax is due September 1 for the current tax year, and bills for 2026 become delinquent on January 6, 2027. The county mails bills in late July to early August, and money received before September 1 can earn a discount.

If you sold the property after receiving a bill, the Collections page says to forward the bill to the new owner unless you intend to pay it. Agreements between buyers, sellers and attorneys are not the tax office's concern, and because tax is a lien on real estate, the buyer wants everything settled at closing. A mortgage company that escrows tax still causes the bill to be mailed to the owner, and the county suggests checking in the second week of September that the lender paid. The county also bills a Solid Waste Availability Fee for each electrical connection, set each year in the budget ordinance, and it does not depend on full-time residence.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Franklin County property value?
sections.html:
File the Board of Equalization and Review appeal form any time after January 1 until the board adjourns, usually in May, or within 30 days of a value change notice.

Staff review comes first, and cases they cannot settle go to the board, which mails its decision. The current revaluation took effect January 1, 2024, so the county looks for evidence tied to that date. Reasons that have no legal basis include a tax bill that went up, a fixed income, or a drop in market prices after January 1, 2024. Reasons the county accepts include similar properties with lower values, comparable sales before that date, unrepaired storm or fire damage, a denied septic permit and documented environmental cleanup costs. The owner carries the burden of proof. Ask the tax office about relief programs if the concern is affordability rather than value.

sections.h2: Why does recording order matter on a Franklin County sale?
sections.html:
In North Carolina a conveyance, option, lease over three years or similar interest is valid against lien creditors and buyers for value only from the time it is registered in the county where the land lies. Priority follows the order and time of registration (G.S. 47-18).

For a seller this is the reason closings are timed around the recording cutoff, and the reason an unrecorded deed from a prior owner can stall a new sale. If an inherited Franklin County house still shows a deceased relative on record, the missing step is usually a recorded estate document, so check the Register of Deeds index before you list and ask your closing attorney what must be recorded first.

faqs.q: Is the Franklin County Register of Deeds in the courthouse?
faqs.a: No, not at present. The office now sits at 283-B S. Bickett Boulevard in Louisburg while the courthouse is under construction. Mail goes to P.O. Box 545, Louisburg, NC 27549, and the phone is 919-496-3500.

faqs.q: Do I need a tax certification stamp to record a deed in Franklin County?
faqs.a: Yes for a deed transferring real property. The Tax Collector must certify that no delinquent taxes are a lien on the parcel, and the service is free on weekdays from 8 am to 5 pm. eRecording routes the deed to the tax office for you, with a 4:30 pm cutoff for stamped items.

faqs.q: What is the Franklin County deed recording fee?
faqs.a: It follows the state schedule: $26.00 for the first 15 pages of an ordinary instrument and $64.00 for the first 35 pages of a deed of trust, with $4.00 for each added page in both cases. Ask the office to confirm before you send a long document.

faqs.q: Can a title company record electronically in Franklin County?
faqs.a: Yes. The office accepts all document types electronically except UCC filings, through CSC, Simplifile or the ePN network. The company or closing attorney normally handles the submission.

faqs.q: Who pays the North Carolina deed excise tax?
faqs.a: The transferor, who is the seller, pays it to the register of deeds before the deed is recorded. The rate is $1.00 per $500.00 or fractional part of the price or value. Your settlement statement shows the amount.
